lines.text: A steel bar sinks instantly. So how does a ship made of thousands of tons of that steel float?
Anything in water gets pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside.
A solid block of steel pushes aside only a little water, much less than its own weight, so it sinks.
Shape that same steel into a hollow hull, and it pushes aside far more water.
Most of a ship's inside is air, so its average density ends up lower than water's.
It settles until the water it displaces weighs exactly as much as the ship.
That's why ships carry load lines, called Plimsoll marks, showing how deep they can safely sit. In fresh water, they ride lower.
